summary: Defines an extension to SDP and RTP that lets a media stream be looped back to its sender. Operators can use it to monitor voice, text and video quality and to test the delivery path of real-time services.

plainLanguage.summary: You shout into a canyon and listen to the echo to check how well your voice travelled. This lets a call echo itself back for testing.

questions: how to test voip quality by looping media back
what is the difference between rtp-pkt-loopback and rtp-media-loopback
subtitle: SDP attributes and RTP payload formats that let a call echo its own media back for quality testing.

tldr.problem: Operators of VoIP, real-time text and video services have little beyond ping and traceroute to actively monitor media quality to the edge of a service.
tldr.mechanism: Three SDP attributes (loopback, loopback-source, loopback-mirror) negotiate through offer/answer which side sends and which side echoes media, at packet level (two RTP payload formats) or at media level after decoding.
tldr.outcome: A tested endpoint can be asked to mirror media on demand, with RTCP and RTCP-XR reporting the results, but loopback needs safeguards against abuse such as authentication and rate limiting.

facts.label: Minimum implementation
facts.value: rtp-pkt-loopback with direct loopback; offerer can be source

today: RFC 6849 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Loop Media Back
sections.content:
Quality of VoIP, real-time text and video services depends on the media path. One way to watch it is active monitoring: ask an endpoint to loop media back to the other endpoint and report statistics such as RTCP and RTCP-XR information.

The alternative, special endpoints that always loop media back, works but does not scale to large networks, adds network management work, and cannot test one specific endpoint that may be having trouble. This RFC defines new SDP media types and attributes, uses the SDP offer/answer model (RFC 3264) to set up the loopback, and gives guidance on RTP (RFC 3550) and RTCP reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building a special echo room that echoes everyone, you ask the exact friend you want to test to echo your voice back.

sections.title: Roles and Three Use Cases
sections.content:
Packets flow from the loopback source to the loopback mirror, which returns them. The peers settle roles and loopback type in advance using the SDP offer/answer exchange. Three use cases differ in how the mirror treats incoming RTP packets:

  • Encapsulated packet loopback: the whole incoming RTP packet becomes the payload of a new outer RTP packet. The source can compute one-way statistics for each direction and can play back the content. The larger packet may hit MTU limits, so RTP-level fragmentation is offered.
  • Direct loopback: the mirror copies only the payload into a new RTP packet. Packet size stays the same both ways and there is no fragmentation, but the source can compute only two-way statistics from the header.
  • Media loopback: the mirror decodes the packet, taking it as close as possible to the analog level, then re-encodes it in a format chosen by SDP negotiation. This allows troubleshooting at the codec level, with path statistics limited to what RTCP reports provide.
sections.plainLanguage: The echo can repeat your whole letter with the envelope, just the words inside, or a retelling after the friend understood it and said it again.

sections.title: Negotiating Loopback in SDP
sections.content:
Three media-level SDP attributes are defined. a=loopback:<loopback-type> carries one or more types: rtp-pkt-loopback (packet level, covering encapsulated and direct loopback) or rtp-media-loopback (media level). a=loopback-source says the sender is the media source and expects the receiver to mirror. a=loopback-mirror says the sender will echo all received media and generates no media of its own.

An offerer includes both a type and a role attribute for each media description it wants looped back. To accept, the answerer includes both attributes, with the opposite role. If several types are offered, the answer MUST include only one, and the answerer SHOULD prefer the first listed. For rtp-pkt-loopback, the offer MUST also carry the encaprtp or rtploopback encoding name, or both.

An answerer rejects loopback by setting the stream's port to zero or rejecting the whole offer. If the answer lacks any loopback attribute, the remote side is assumed not to support the extension, which is not a protocol failure. The directions recvonly and sendonly MUST NOT be used; inactive disables loopback, and either side may send a new offer to switch between normal and loopback mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the echo game, one side says "I will talk" and the other says "I will echo". The echoer can say no by hanging up that part of the call.

sections.title: RTP and the Two Payload Formats
sections.content:
A loopback source MUST NOT send multiple source streams on the same 5-tuple, because the mirror cannot say which is which. For rtp-media-loopback, the mirror MUST transmit all received media back unless congestion feedback or lower-layer limits prevent it. It treats the media as if it were to be played (for example, applying packet loss concealment) and regenerates all RTP header fields.

For packet loopback, the encapsulated format adds a payload header in front of the original RTP header and payload. It starts with a 4-byte receive timestamp, and a 2-bit Fragmentation field takes the place of the first two bits of the original header: 00 first fragment, 01 last fragment, 10 no fragmentation, 11 intermediate fragment. Its dynamic payload type is bound to the name encaprtp.

The direct loopback format defines no payload header; the mirror simply copies the payload data. Because the original payload type is lost, the source SHOULD send only one payload type per loopback session in this mode. Its name is rtploopback, also with a dynamic payload type. The RFC cites the 16-byte overhead of the encapsulated format as the reason to choose direct loopback.
sections.plainLanguage: Encapsulated loopback sends back the whole letter with its envelope plus a note of when it arrived. Direct loopback sends back only the letter, which is lighter.

sections.title: NAT, SRTP, RTCP and Congestion
sections.content:
NATs: ICE, TURN and STUN apply where possible. Without ICE, a mirror behind a NAT sends no RTP of its own, so it MUST send some packets to the peer to open the NAT pinhole. Symmetric RTP/RTCP MUST be used unless the mirror can control the NATs on its path.

SRTP (RFC 3711) MAY be used. The mirror loops back after decrypting and authenticating, then encrypts with its own key. If used, it MUST be used in both directions with the same properties.

RTCP: since the purpose is monitoring, agents SHOULD support RTCP and RTCP-XR (RFC 3611), including the Loss RLE, Duplicate RLE, Statistics Summary and VoIP Metrics report blocks.

Congestion: participants in media-level loopback SHOULD implement congestion control for the RTP profile in use. For packet-level loopback, the source SHOULD do it, reducing its sending rate to cover both the forward and reverse paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The echoer may have to knock first so the door lets the echo through. Secret messages stay secret both ways, and the speaker slows down if the road gets jammed.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Examples
sections.content:
In the RFC's first example, an offerer sends m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0 with a=loopback:rtp-media-loopback and a=loopback-source. The answer carries a=loopback-mirror with the same type, agreeing to mirror at media level.

In the second, the offerer lists rtp-media-loopback rtp-pkt-loopback plus encaprtp and rtploopback payload types. The answerer picks rtp-pkt-loopback and the encapsulated format. In the third, the answerer sets the media port to 0 to reject the loopback stream.
sections.plainLanguage: One side says "I will talk, please echo me". The other says "OK, I will echo" or "no thanks".

sections.title: Security Risks of Echoing
sections.content:
Loopback can be automated without the user's knowledge, so answerers should watch for denial-of-service attacks. The RFC RECOMMENDS authenticating loopback session requests and limiting their frequency.

It describes several attacks. If signaling is unauthenticated, an attacker could set up a session where two victims each act as rtp-pkt-loopback mirrors for each other, so a few packets loop between them endlessly. A mirror can also be used as indirection to reflect an attacker's packets at a target the attacker could not reach directly. On mobile phones, unauthenticated loopback could drain the battery or cause data fees.

End-user devices SHOULD indicate to the user that a loopback session is active, even an authenticated one, and devices SHOULD use keepalive tests or time out sessions automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could make two people echo each other forever. So only let trusted people start the echo game, and stop it after a while.

sections.title: Minimum Implementation and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC calls the approach a complete solution that may be too heavy for some implementations. All implementations MUST at least support rtp-pkt-loopback with the direct loopback payload encoding, and an SDP offerer MUST at least be able to act as a loopback source.

IANA registered the three SDP attributes and the media types audio/encaprtp, video/encaprtp and text/encaprtp, among others in the full registrations, each with a required rate parameter and intended usage LIMITED USE.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must at least be able to play the simplest version of the echo game.
